title: A lesson for those with minds
hook: in their stories is a lesson for people of understanding (12:111)

segments.voice: Yesterday, reading it whole: the dream, the shirt three times, sabrun jamil, beautiful patience, twice. Your line was read it whole. Did you find the time for Surah Yusuf? Day four hundred forty-one, the end of a week.

This week was a parade of people. The mighty 'Ad, told that forgiveness is strength. Thamud and the she-camel. Ibrahim's roasted calf and Lut in his doorway. Shu'ayb and the honest scales. Then Yusuf, the best of stories, read whole. That's a lot of stories for one week. So what are they for? The very last verse of Surah Yusuf answers that, and not just for Yusuf. It looks back over everything, the prophets of Surah Hud included, and says what a reader is supposed to do with a story once it's over.

Verse one hundred eleven, in Pickthall's translation: "In their history verily there is a lesson for men of understanding." Two Arabic words carry it. The first is 'ibra, a lesson. Its root, '-b-r, means to cross over, the way you cross a river. 'Ubur is a crossing. And the same root gives ta'bir, the interpreting of dreams, which runs all through this surah: Yusuf crosses over from the picture in the dream to what it means. So an 'ibra is a lesson you get by crossing over: from their story to your life, from what happened to them to what it means for you. The second word is albab, minds, the plural of lubb. Lubb is the core of a thing, the kernel inside the shell. Ulu al-albab, people with minds, are people who get to the core. The verse goes on: this isn't an invented tale, but a confirmation of what came before it, a detailed explanation of everything, and a guidance and a mercy for people who believe. So the Qur'an doesn't tell stories just to pass the evening, or to make you wonder how it ends. It tells them so you'll cross over. Yusuf's brothers, jealous of a favored child: is there a jealousy in your house? The woman who lied, then confessed: is there a truth you've been holding back? A father who said beautiful patience twice: what are you waiting through right now? The story is told so that the one hearing it can step into it, and come out somewhere else.
screen: `'IBRA — A LESSON, A CROSSING.` · `TA'BIR — INTERPRETING DREAMS.` · `LUBB — THE CORE, THE KERNEL.` · `FROM THEIR STORY TO YOUR LIFE.` · then, large: `THE STORY IS THE LESSON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one lesson from Yusuf. Sit, and breathe. Let the story pass in front of you: the dream, the well, the house, the prison, the palace, the brothers bowing. Where does it touch your life? Let one lesson come, in your own words, a single sentence. Don't make it grand. When the bell ends, write it down somewhere you'll see it. If you pray, you can ask to understand it. The bell holds the time.
'Ibra. A lesson you cross over into, from their story to your life, the word that closes Surah Yusuf. Today's word.
Your line: the story is the lesson. Today, read the sentence you wrote, once in the morning and once at night. Day four hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers close a study of Surah Yusuf with 12:111 and ask students to draw lessons, 'ibar, from the story for their own lives; the phrase ulu al-albab recurs throughout the Qur'an for people of reflection.
